transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-10-25
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marta Lopez (Nebula VP Eng), Jon Park (Nebula SRE), Sara Kim (Nebula Security), Tariq Ahmed (Nebula PM)

Auto-summary: quick console walkthrough focusing on tracing, error analysis, and request-logs. Showed live demo of tracing waterfalls, error sparkline, and how to export logs for on-prem analysis.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Alex from Redwood. Quick intro, we got Priya from our S E and then from Nebula?
[00:08] Marta Lopez: Hi, Marta here. We're excited — been seeing some weird tail latency in production especially on the question-answering endpoint.
[00:15] Jon Park: Yeah we get occasional spikes at the 95th and 99th, hard to repro locally.
[00:20] Priya Nair: Great, that's exactly what tracing + request logs can help with, we'll show the waterfall, span breakdown and how request logs link back to traces.
[00:30] Sara Kim: Also quick heads up, security team will want to see SOC2, K M S integration, and where request logs live.
[00:37] Alex Chen: Totally, we'll cover where logs are stored and the export flow, and i'll follow up with the compliance pack.
[00:44] Tariq Ahmed: Our timeline is tight — looking to decide next quarter for dedicated capacity.
[00:50] Alex Chen: Understood. We'll highlight how dedicated vs hosted changes latency variability and what metrics to check.

[02:05] Priya Nair: Ok jumping into the Console — first screen is traces list, you can filter by route, model version, and error tag. Notice here the waterfall view, each bar is a span we capture: token generation, KV cache hit, model kernel time, network.
[02:28] Marta Lopez: That KV cache label sometimes shows as "K V cash" in the transcript but we know it's KV cache, right?
[02:34] Priya Nair: Yeah transcription sometimes garbles it. The important bit is the span durations. See this request at 10:12AM with a long tail around 1.2s on the model kernel stage.
[02:45] Jon Park: Can you open the request logs for that trace id?
[02:48] Priya Nair: Sure — request logs panel links to the raw request with headers, token counts, latency breakdown and any retries. You can export as ndjson or download a zip if you want to ship to on-prem for deeper analysis.
[03:05] Alex Chen: Note that for PII-sensitive workloads we can mask tokens at ingest and only store aggregates, and we also integrate with customer KMS so logs can be encrypted at rest.
[03:15] Sara Kim: How does that KMS integration look? Is it customer managed?
[03:20] Alex Chen: Yes, you can bring your own keys via K M S/H S M — we'll document the steps, it's part of the private deployment and available for Dedicated as well.

[04:30] Priya Nair: Back to traces — you'll often see repeated short model kernel spans when we batch requests, the console collapses similar spans to make slow tails obvious. See the orange spike here, that's an error rate bump correlated with a model fallback.
[04:50] Marta Lopez: Model fallback? Like switching to a cheaper variant during load? We had a vendor who did that and responses changed.
[04:58] Priya Nair: Exactly, Redwood can be configured with routing policies — for latency critical paths you pin a single model version or set a no-fallback policy. We showed an example of an automatic fallback in the trace where a fallback added 400ms.

[06:10] Jon Park: For debugging, can we search traces by header values? We send X-Correlation-Id from our service.
[06:16] Priya Nair: Yes, you can filter traces by custom attributes including X-Correlation-Id or user id. When you click a trace we show linked request logs with full header annotation.
[06:25] Jon Park: Nice. If we export logs, do we get raw token strings? Our security team will ask to avoid that.
[06:32] Alex Chen: By default we store token metadata and counts; you can enable token redaction so raw tokens are not persisted. We'll include that in the compliance packet.

[08:00] Priya Nair: Next, error analysis — Console aggregates errors by route and model, shows stack traces for infra-level failures and model-level rejects. Here's a common reject we see for bad input, the error panel links you to the offending request and the prompt snippet.
[08:20] Marta Lopez: Sometimes the errors show as "403 model reject" but our logs show downstream 502; can they map?
[08:27] Priya Nair: We surface both the Redwood service error and the downstream status; the error timeline helps you see if it's a model reject preceding a proxy 502 or vice versa.

[10:02] Alex Chen: We also have a request replay feature in the Console for internal debugging — replays are sent to a sandbox model variant so you don't hit production traffic. Useful for reproducing flakiness.
[10:15] Tariq Ahmed: Is the replay data stored? Any retention concerns?
[10:18] Alex Chen: Replays are ephemeral; you can configure retention windows for request logs and set deletion policies via the Console or API.

[12:00] Jon Park: Let's talk about the slow tail — we often see 99th percentile spikes that correlate with long kernel times. How do you recommend investigating?
[12:08] Priya Nair: Start with traces sorted by p99 latency, inspect model kernel span distribution; check if KV cache hit rate drops for those traces — if cache miss, kernel work increases. Also check batching metrics: oversized batches can push tokens through slower kernels, increasing variability.
[12:30] Marta Lopez: Is there a way to proactively alert on KV cache degradation?
[12:34] Priya Nair: Yes, Console has alerting hooks for metrics like KV cache hit rate, model kernel latency, and error rates. We can demo setting a canary alert in a follow-up.

[15:00] Priya Nair: Now i'll show a live debug flow: filter to route /qa-v1, time range 09:50-10:30, apply tag error=timeout. See these three traces, first one shows prefix caching enabled but a cache miss, second has a model fallback, third shows network retry.
[15:25] Marta Lopez: The second trace shows a large token count — we had a prompt expansion issue this week that accidentally concatenated a history.
[15:33] Priya Nair: Right, token count is surfaced and there's a token histogram per trace. You can click into the request log to see the prompt and which assistant messages were included.

[18:00] Alex Chen: A quick note on cost. Console breaks down per-request cost by tokenization, model runtime, and egress, so you can see expensive routes and consider quantization or batching changes.
[18:15] Marta Lopez: Curious — have customers used Optimize recommendations to reduce cost without hurting quality?
[18:20] Alex Chen: Yes, Optimize suggests quantization profiles and batching settings per-route based on your traffic pattern. We can share some anonymous before/after numbers with the pilot.

[20:10] Sara Kim: Back to compliance, how do we get audit logs for who accessed traces? We need RBAC and audit trails for the security review.
[20:18] Alex Chen: Console has audit logs with user-level access events and API key usage. You can configure S S O (SAML) and role-based access to restrict who sees PII or raw prompts.

[22:45] Priya Nair: I'll demonstrate trace-to-log correlation: click a trace span, open the right panel, and then click 'Open request in logs' — the request log shows headers, response codes, latency samples, and any attached error payloads.
[23:05] Jon Park: If we want raw logs shipped to our SIEM, do you support streaming?
[23:10] Priya Nair: Yes, we support streaming exports to S3/Cloud Storage or direct ship to SIEM via webhook. There's also a connector for Kafka if you run on-prem.

[25:30] Marta Lopez: Our main risk is data residency — can logs be kept in our cloud region only?
[25:36] Alex Chen: For Dedicated and Private deployments, yes — you can choose region-specific storage and private networking. Hosted API stores logs in-region as an option; we'll confirm specifics in the compliance docs we send.

[28:00] Priya Nair: Demoing request logs export: choose time range, apply filter X-Correlation-Id, export ndjson, here's a sample with request_id, model_version, token_count, latency_ms. Note that PII is redacted if you turned on token redaction.
[28:25] Tariq Ahmed: Can we run a pilot where Redwood ingests a week's worth of production traces and you help us identify hotspots?
[28:31] Alex Chen: Absolutely, typical pilot is 2-4 weeks, we run a benchmark and provide a tuning plan — suggests batching, quantization, and routing tweaks. We'll scope around your peak traffic windows.

[30:40] Priya Nair: One small caveat: if you enable very aggressive batching to reduce cost, you might see higher tail latency under bursty traffic; Optimize can suggest a sweet spot.
[30:50] Jon Park: That tradeoff is exactly what we're worried about. We'll want to test with our spike patterns.

[33:00] Alex Chen: Wrapping up, we'll send the SOC2 and network diagram, Priya will send the tracing queries and a short how-to doc, Marta will send a bundle of failing request IDs and logs. We'll draft a pilot SOW if Nebula wants Dedicated capacity testing.
[33:20] Marta Lopez: Sounds good. Can you also include estimated costs for a 2-week dedicated pilot?
[33:27] Alex Chen: Yes, i'll include a sample pricing calc with expected token volume and reserved capacity delta.

[35:00] Sara Kim: Quick question — do you support encrypted search over logs or will the SIEM handle that?
[35:06] Priya Nair: For now SIEM handles encrypted search; we can advise on tokenization strategies to minimize sensitive material in logs.

[38:10] Jon Park: Any known issues with multi-region routing causing slight increases in latency? We saw something like that when we tested with another vendor.
[38:18] Priya Nair: Multi-region routing can add hops if not anchored; Redwood's smart routing prefers pinned regions for a customer when possible. We'll show routing policies in the Console in the pilot.

[41:00] Alex Chen: Ok final recap of next steps and owners: SOC2 and network diagram from us, tracing queries from Priya, sample logs from Nebula. We'll target initial pilot week of 2026-11-09, pending your sign-off.
[41:20] Marta Lopez: We'll aim to have our logs to you by 2026-10-29. Thanks for the walkthrough.
[41:30] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the requested artifacts.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcript quality: automated captions had occasional mis-attributions and minor word swaps (e.g., K V cache -> KV cache, S S O -> SSO).
